title: Lesson 26: The Manager's Guide: Running a Company-wide Rollout
description: Why handing out licenses is not a rollout, when a group's rules and owner have to be in place, and which training design actually moves adoption.

questions.question: A company buys licenses for everyone and announces that the tool is available. Why is that not a rollout?
options: It skips the vendor evaluation step entirely
It hands out access without changing how people work
It costs more than a phased approach would
It leaves the tool undocumented for new hires
questions.explanation: Distribution delivers access. A rollout changes the default way work gets done, which takes sequencing, training, and controls rather than flipping a switch.

questions.question: When should a new department's data rules and named owner be in place?
options: Before that department starts using the tool
After the first month, once real problems appear
Once the number of users passes a hundred
Whenever the legal review finishes, regardless of users
questions.explanation: Users multiply faster than controls if you let them. Each group needs its rules, approved tool, and owner established before it starts, or the rollout becomes an uncontrolled experiment.

questions.question: Which training design fits what is known about who gains most from an AI assistant?
options: A single full-day workshop for the whole company
Written documentation sent to everyone at launch
Short daily practice on real work, aimed hardest at the least experienced
Advanced sessions reserved for the highest performers
questions.explanation: Gains concentrate among newer and less experienced people, and they come from repeated practice on real tasks. Little and often reaches them better than one long session.
